text: You now have the full model from the last three lessons: seven tenets, and the Policy Engine, Policy Administrator, and Policy Enforcement Point that carry them out. Almost everything else you'll hear in Zero Trust conversations is either a synonym for one of those pieces, an input the trust algorithm uses, or a product category implementing one of those roles. This lesson is the glossary that proves it.

Restated in the vocabulary you'll actually hear: the subject is just the principal making the request — the same thing you've modeled in every IAM request so far. The Policy Decision Point is NIST's name for the PE and PA working together, which in practice looks like Conditional Access evaluating a policy and then issuing the resulting token. The PEP is whatever sits on the connection path enforcing that decision — a ZTNA gateway, a SASE edge, or an AWS Verified Access endpoint.

The trust algorithm's inputs get their own acronyms too, but you've already built every one of them. CDM is continuous device posture, the same job Intune or AWS Systems Manager already does. PKI is your certificate authority. ICAM is your identity provider and its lifecycle processes from course eight. Threat intelligence and activity logs are exactly the SIEM and XDR pipelines you built as a SOC analyst, just feeding forward into a decision instead of sitting in a dashboard.

ZTNA, SASE, and micro-segmentation aren't separate frameworks competing with this model — they're packaged implementations of it. ZTNA replaces broad VPN access with per-application PEP enforcement. SASE bundles several PEP-style controls into one cloud-delivered edge. Micro-segmentation pushes that same PEP enforcement down to small internal zones, closing off east-west traffic instead of leaving it as an implicit trust zone.

That's the whole vocabulary problem solved the same way, five times over: component, input, or implementation category. Every later lesson in this capstone — identity-centric segmentation, cloud workload identity, continuous verification — is a deeper dive into one row of these tables, not new content. Chapter 2 starts applying this model to a real architecture.
